434	##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-024.md
435	# ADR-024: Windows ACL hardening at install time via `icacls`, not in the daemon
436	
437	## Status
438	
439	Accepted
440	
441	## Date
442	
443	2026-06-11
444	
445	## Context
446	
447	The Unix daemon binary applies `chmod 0o700` to `$FFS_DATA_DIR/run/` at startup (`crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs`) so a malicious local process can't swap the UDS file out from under us between bind and accept. That's a defense-in-depth check sitting on top of the OS's per-user home-directory protections.
448	
449	Windows has no `chmod`. The closest equivalent is to write a DACL granting Full Control to the current user and nothing to anyone else. Two implementation sites were considered for task_34:
450	
451	- **Option A — daemon-side.** Call `SetNamedSecurityInfoW` from `crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs` via `windows-sys`. Pros: enforcement runs every daemon boot, even if the user side-stepped the installer. Cons: pulls a large platform crate into the daemon for what is effectively a setup-time concern; the ACL code lives in main.rs forever and needs to be maintained alongside the Unix path.
452	
453	- **Option B — installer-side.** Have `installer/install.ps1` invoke `icacls` once at install time to lock down `$FFS_DATA_DIR` (and its `run/` subdirectory) to the current user. Pros: matches the Unix story exactly (the *installer* runs `chmod 0o700`, not the daemon — `installer/install.sh` already does this). Keeps the daemon binary platform-agnostic. Cons: someone who deletes the ACL between install and boot gets an unhardened directory until the next install.
454	
455	## Decision
456	
457	Task_34 uses **Option B (installer-side `icacls`)**.
458	
459	`installer/install.ps1` invokes `icacls "$DataDir" /inheritance:r /grant:r "$env:USERNAME:(OI)(CI)F"` on the data root and the `run/` subdirectory after creating them. The daemon's `main.rs` leaves the existing `#[cfg(unix)]` `chmod 0o700` block alone and adds no Windows counterpart.
460	
461	## Alternatives Considered
462	
463	### Option A — daemon-side `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`
464	
465	- **Description:** The daemon binary calls `windows-sys` ACL APIs to harden `$FFS_DATA_DIR/run/` at every startup.
466	- **Pros:** Re-enforces hardening on every boot. Survives an ACL deletion between install and boot.
467	- **Cons:** Adds a meaningful Windows-only dependency (`windows-sys` Win32::Security feature set, ~300 KB of generated bindings) to the daemon binary for what is fundamentally a setup-time concern. Asymmetric with the Unix story where the chmod lives in the *installer*, not the daemon — Unix's `installer/install.sh` already does `chmod 0o700 "$DATA_DIR"`. The daemon-side Unix chmod at `main.rs:135` is an additional belt-and-braces guard specifically on the socket's parent dir, not the data dir.
468	- **Why rejected:** The dep-weight + complexity asymmetry isn't worth re-enforcement on every boot. A user who manually clears the ACL has bigger problems and will see the next install fix it.
469	
470	### Option C — neither (rely on `$LOCALAPPDATA` / `$USERPROFILE` defaults)
471	
472	- **Description:** Skip explicit ACL hardening; trust that Windows' default ACL on `%USERPROFILE%\.ffs\` (inherited from the user profile) already restricts to the current user.
473	- **Pros:** Zero installer code, zero daemon code, no platform deps.
474	- **Cons:** Default ACLs on `%USERPROFILE%` may inherit broader rights from parent folders depending on Group Policy / domain configuration / OEM image. Defense-in-depth is exactly the place to not rely on environmental defaults — that's why the Unix daemon does `chmod 0o700` *on top of* the home-directory default.
475	- **Why rejected:** Equivalent posture to the Unix story is the goal; "trust the default" doesn't meet it.
476	
477	## Consequences
478	
479	### Positive
480	
481	- Daemon binary stays platform-agnostic. No `windows-sys` dep, no `#[cfg(windows)]` ACL block in `main.rs`.
482	- Story matches Unix: the installer hardens the data dir; the daemon trusts that hardening at runtime.
483	- `icacls` is a stock Windows command — no PowerShell module dependency, works on every supported Windows since 7.
484	
485	### Negative
486	
487	- An adversary who clears the ACL between install and daemon boot gets an unhardened state until the next install runs. The mitigation is "users who alter their data dir's ACL get what they ask for."
488	
489	### Risks
490	
491	- **`icacls` semantics edge cases.** `icacls` flag combinations are notoriously fiddly; the chosen `/inheritance:r /grant:r "<user>:(OI)(CI)F"` form has the specific effect of "remove inherited permissions, grant the current user Full Control with Object Inherit + Container Inherit." Verified via the `icacls "$Dir"` output post-install — the install.ps1 step is followed by a verification call.
492	- **Service vs. interactive identity.** If the user later registers the daemon as a Windows service rather than the at-logon scheduled task that install.ps1 wires up, the running identity differs from `$env:USERNAME`. That's out of scope for MVP (the installer uses the scheduled-task path) but should be revisited if a service installer lands.
493	
494	## Implementation Notes
495	
496	The `icacls` invocation lives in `installer/install.ps1`:
497	
498	```powershell
499	function Harden-Acl($path) {
500	    if ($DryRun) {
501	        Write-Host "+ icacls $path /inheritance:r /grant:r `"$env:USERNAME`":(OI)(CI)F"
502	    } else {
503	        & icacls $path /inheritance:r /grant:r "$($env:USERNAME):(OI)(CI)F" | Out-Null
504	    }
505	}
506	
507	Harden-Acl $DataDir
508	Harden-Acl (Join-Path $DataDir 'run')
509	```
510	
511	The flags decompose as:
512	
513	- `/inheritance:r` — remove inherited ACEs from the target. Without this, ACEs from `$env:USERPROFILE` (or further up if domain-joined) propagate.
514	- `/grant:r "user:(OI)(CI)F"` — replace any existing ACE for `user` with `Full Control`, applied to this folder, subfolders (Container Inherit), and files within (Object Inherit).
515	
516	## References
517	
518	- See `installer/install.sh` for the Unix sibling that does `chmod 0o700 "$DATA_DIR"`.
519	- See `crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs` for the daemon-side `chmod 0o700` on `run/` (Unix-only).
520	- See task_34 for the broader Windows daemon-path correctness work that this ADR is a piece of.
521	- Microsoft documentation: `icacls` flag reference — `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/icacls`.
522	##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-026.md
523	# ADR-026: Scribe v2 — predicate-schema-driven extraction with pluggable engines
524	
525	## Status
526	
527	Accepted
528	
529	## Date
530	
531	2026-06-21
532	
533	## Context
534	
535	The scribe skill (task_11, refined in task_32) extracts structured proposals from free-text notes dropped into `ingest/`. Its extraction logic is regex heuristics: a `[A-Z][a-z]+\s+[A-Z][a-z]+` bigram scan for names, pattern detectors for phones/emails, a stop-word list, venue masking. Live use on 2026-06-21 produced the canonical failure: a file named `Jon Jones.md` containing a key-value contact card (`Nickname: Bones / Occupation: UFC fighter / Phone numbe r- 9194284074`) was extracted as a `contact.person` with **`display_name: "Bones Occupation"`** — two random title-case words stitched across lines. Five distinct failure modes were catalogued (filename ignored, key-value card shape unrecognized, field labels treated as name candidates, no cross-check against the filename, verbatim typo propagation).
536	
537	The deeper diagnosis: **this is not a regex-quality problem, it is an architecture problem.** Two structural facts make the current design wrong regardless of how clever the patterns get:
538	
539	1. **Scribe ignores the predicate registry.** FFS predicates are defined in TOML specs carrying real JSON Schemas (`claim_schema` blocks) — the substrate already knows, in machine-readable form, exactly what shapes it can hold. The scribe hardcodes `contact.person` and `note` logic instead of consuming those schemas. Every new predicate the user registers is invisible to extraction until someone hand-writes new regexes.
540	2. **The quality ceiling of pattern-matching is far below what the substrate needs.** "Records-shaped substrate for personal knowledge" is the project thesis; the scribe is the front door through which records enter. A front door that guesses names from capitalized bigrams caps the entire system's usefulness.
541	
542	The decision below resolves a question that blocked progress for roughly two months: which extraction technology, given the tension between quality (frontier LLM APIs), privacy (personal records leaving the machine), and operational weight (local model installs). The resolution came from noticing that **four of the five blocking sub-questions answer themselves from constraints already committed in this repository**:
543	
544	| Blocking question | Answer, and where it was already decided |
545	|---|---|
546	| Is "records never leave the machine" a hard line? | Wrong framing. The distinction that matters is **ambient vs. invoked**. The substrate is SQLCipher-encrypted and local-first, but `ffs-mcp` (task_16) exists precisely so Claude can read the substrate when the user invokes it. A daemon that silently ships every note to an API is ambient exfiltration; a user-configured engine choice is invocation. Resolution: **local-only default, cloud backend as explicit opt-in configuration.** The blocker dissolves from a decision into a setting. |
547	| Extraction scope — contacts, or everything? | The predicate registry answers this. Extraction must target **whatever predicates are registered**, driven by their `claim_schema`s. Hardcoding any predicate shape is the bug being fixed, not a scope option. |
548	| Latency budget? | Non-issue. The ingest stability window (task_31, 30 s) plus the asynchronous quarantine mean extraction latency is invisible below ~30 s. Quality wins every latency tradeoff available. |
549	| Acceptable dependencies? | ADR-009 is decisive: skill bundles are **stdlib-only, zero pip dependencies**. This *eliminates* classical NER (spaCy/GLiNER require torch) and *selects* LLM-over-HTTP: both the Anthropic Messages API and a localhost Ollama server are plain JSON-over-HTTP, callable with `urllib.request` from the standard library. Python 3.11+ `tomllib` likewise reads the predicate TOMLs with zero deps. |
550	| Feedback/correction loop? | Already exists — the quarantine's accept/reject flow (tasks 19, 29). Record which engine+model produced each proposal in provenance; defer fine-tuning on accept/reject history to post-MVP. |
551	
552	## Decision
553	
554	Scribe v2 restructures extraction around two seams:
555	
556	**1. Engine abstraction.** An `ExtractionEngine` interface inside the skill bundle (stdlib-only Python), with two implementations:
557	
558	- **`heuristic`** — today's regex code, refactored behind the interface. Always available, fully offline, zero configuration. **Remains the default.**
559	- **`llm`** — a stdlib-`urllib` HTTP client with two thin backend adapters:
560	  - **Ollama** (`http://localhost:11434/api/chat`) — local models, nothing leaves the machine; for users who install Ollama.
561	  - **Anthropic Messages API** (`https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`) — highest quality ceiling; explicit opt-in; API key via environment or OS keychain.
562	
563	  Selection via `FFS_SCRIBE_ENGINE` (`heuristic` | `llm`), backend via `FFS_SCRIBE_LLM_URL` + `FFS_SCRIBE_LLM_MODEL`. Any `llm` failure (network down, malformed output, schema-invalid JSON) falls back to `heuristic` so ingest never hard-fails on connectivity.
564	
565	**2. Predicate-schema-driven prompts.** The extraction prompt is **generated from the registered predicate specs** — the skill reads the TOMLs from `$FFS_DATA_DIR/config/predicates/` via stdlib `tomllib` and renders each predicate's name, `claim_schema`, and description into the instruction. LLM output is validated against the same `claim_schema` before becoming a proposal. Consequences: adding a predicate extends extraction automatically; the schema is enforced at both ends; the heuristic engine remains the only place with per-predicate hand-written logic (and only as fallback).
566	
567	Supporting decisions:
568	
569	- **Provenance** on every proposal gains `engine` + `model` fields, surfaced in the quarantine review UI so the user can calibrate trust per engine.
570	- **A golden-corpus evaluation harness** (~20 fixture notes including the Jon Jones card, each with expected proposals) scores engines objectively via pytest. Heuristic-engine scores gate CI; LLM-engine scoring runs out-of-band (requires network/models). This converts "the scribe guessed wrong again" into a measured, regression-tested engineering surface.
571	- **The quarantine remains the human gate.** No proposal commits without user accept, regardless of engine.
572	
573	## Alternatives Considered
574	
575	### Alternative 1: Keep improving the heuristics (regex++)
576	
577	- **Description:** Add filename consultation, key-value card detection, extended stop-lists, cross-checks — the five fixes catalogued from the Jon Jones failure.
578	- **Pros:** No new moving parts; fully offline; each fix is small.
579	- **Cons:** Two months of this produced "Bones Occupation." The ceiling is structurally low: every new note shape needs a new hand-written rule, and the registry-blindness is untouched. This is the bandaid path.
580	- **Why rejected as the strategy:** Retained only as (a) the default/fallback engine and (b) a bounded hygiene pass, because the heuristic engine still serves offline users. Rejected as the answer to extraction quality.
581	
582	### Alternative 2: Classical NER (spaCy `en_core_web_trf`, GLiNER, NuExtract)
583	
584	- **Description:** Pretrained token-classification models; ~92% F1 on standard entity types; ~100 ms on Apple Silicon; fully local.
585	- **Pros:** Fast, private, well-understood.
586	- **Cons:** **Violates ADR-009** — these require torch-class pip dependencies inside the skill bundle, or a sidecar model-server that is its own operational burden. Also structurally narrower than the requirement: NER tags entity spans; it does not fill arbitrary registered `claim_schema`s.
587	- **Why rejected:** The ADR-009 constraint alone is disqualifying; the scope mismatch seconds it.
588	
589	### Alternative 3: Local LLM as the only engine (mandatory Ollama)
590	
591	- **Description:** Require Ollama + a 5–15 GB model (e.g., Qwen 2.5 7B) on every install; all extraction runs locally through it.
592	- **Pros:** High quality and private, no cloud dependency.
593	- **Cons:** Forces a heavyweight install on every user of what is meant to be a light, technical-friend-installable substrate (ADR-005's friction-floor argument). Model supervision (updates, disk, RAM) becomes FFS's problem.
594	- **Why rejected as mandatory:** Accepted instead as one *backend* of the `llm` engine for users who choose it.
595	
596	### Alternative 4: Cloud LLM as the only engine (Anthropic-only)
597	
598	- **Description:** All extraction goes through the Anthropic API.
599	- **Pros:** Highest accuracy; simplest single path; the user already trusts Anthropic tooling with this repository.
600	- **Cons:** Ambient transmission of personal records to a third party as a *side effect of dropping a file in a folder* contradicts the local-first, encrypted-at-rest posture the whole substrate is built on. Also fails offline.
601	- **Why rejected as default:** Accepted as the opt-in backend with the strongest quality ceiling; rejected as ambient default.
602	
603	## Consequences
604	
605	### Positive
606	
607	- Extraction quality ceiling moves from "regex bigram guessing" to "frontier LLM with schema-enforced output," at the user's chosen privacy level.
608	- The predicate registry becomes the single source of truth for extractable shapes — registering a predicate extends capture automatically.
609	- The eval corpus makes extraction quality measurable and regression-gated for the first time.
610	- ADR-009 is preserved: everything is stdlib (`urllib`, `json`, `tomllib`); no pip deps enter the bundle.
611	- Offline behavior is never worse than today (heuristic fallback on every `llm` failure).
612	
613	### Negative
614	
615	- Two engines to maintain; the heuristic engine cannot be deleted.
616	- LLM extraction is nondeterministic; the eval harness must score semantically (field-level comparisons with tolerance), not byte-exact.
617	- Prompt rendering from `claim_schema` couples prompt quality to schema quality — poorly-described predicates will extract poorly. (Arguably a feature: it pressures schema hygiene.)
618	- API-key handling adds a small secrets surface (mitigated: reuse the task_27/33 keychain machinery).
619	
620	### Risks
621	
622	- **Small local models may hallucinate fields.** Mitigation: schema validation rejects nonconforming output → heuristic fallback; quarantine catches the rest; eval corpus quantifies per-model reliability before recommending any model.
623	- **Anthropic API shape drift.** Mitigation: the adapter is ~50 lines of stdlib HTTP; version pinned via `anthropic-version` header; failures degrade to heuristic, never to ingest breakage.
624	
625	## Implementation Notes
626	
627	Implementation is scoped in task_36. Key mechanics settled here:
628	
629	- Skill reads predicate TOMLs directly from `$FFS_DATA_DIR/config/predicates/` (stdlib `tomllib`) rather than extending the skills-host protocol — no daemon changes needed for schema access.
630	- Engine + backend config flows as environment variables through the existing daemon → skills-host → subprocess env path.
631	- Heuristic hygiene fixes from the Jon Jones postmortem (filename as name source, `^[A-Z][a-z]+:\s` card-shape detection, field-label stop-words) land as a bounded subtask because the heuristic remains the default engine — explicitly bounded so bandaiding ends here.
632	
633	## References
634	
635	- ADR-009 — skill bundles as claw-shaped, stdlib-only artifacts (the constraint that selected the design).
636	- ADR-005 — friction floor / technical-friend installability (why mandatory Ollama was rejected).
637	- task_11, task_26, task_32 — the scribe lineage this supersedes in approach.
638	- task_16 — `ffs-mcp`, the precedent for invoked (not ambient) Claude access to the substrate.
639	- task_31 — ingest stability window (why latency is a non-issue).
640	- task_36 — the implementation task carrying this decision.
641	- 2026-06-21 "Jon Jones / Bones Occupation" failure postmortem — recorded in task_36's Overview.

##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-009.md
# ADR-009: Claw integration via OpenClaw or Hermes pattern

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-05-05

## Context

FFS's agents — the scribe, the librarian, the auditor, and the courier (Phase 2) — need a host process. The host runs them, manages their identity, mediates their access to LLMs, routes their interactions across user-facing channels (chat, email, voice), and handles operational concerns (lifecycle, resource limits, isolation).

Through 2025-2026, an industry pattern emerged for hosting AI agents on personal hardware: the **claw** pattern. A long-running daemon, multi-channel routing, persistent agent identity and memory, skills as `SKILL.md` artifacts, workspace isolation per agent, bring-your-own-LLM, privacy-default with data on the user's hardware.

OpenClaw (Peter Steinberger, 2025-2026) is the canonical claw implementation, with substantial GitHub adoption. Hermes Agent (Nous Research) is a sibling implementation with a built-in self-improvement loop. NemoClaw (NVIDIA) wraps OpenClaw with policy-based privacy guardrails.

FFS has a choice: build its own agent host, or contribute agent definitions to an existing claw.

## Decision

FFS does not reimplement the claw. FFS contributes **agent definitions** packaged as `SKILL.md`-shaped artifacts that run inside an existing claw (OpenClaw or Hermes). The agent definitions are FFS-specific in that they read from and write to FFS atom storage with FFS semantics; they are claw-pattern compatible in that they're packaged in a format the host can load.

The MVP implementation choice between an OpenClaw integration and a minimal FFS-specific daemon is operational, not architectural. Both are supported by the architecture; the decision is made at implementation time based on the relative maturity of OpenClaw's skill system and the cost of a parallel implementation.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Build FFS's own agent host from scratch

- **Description:** Implement a dedicated FFS daemon that hosts the FFS agents, handles identity and memory, mediates LLM access, etc.
- **Pros:** Full design control. Tight integration with FFS-specific concerns.
- **Cons:** Substantial implementation effort to replicate what OpenClaw and Hermes already do. Doesn't benefit from the claw ecosystem (multi-channel routing, existing skill libraries, user familiarity).
- **Why rejected:** Reinventing existing infrastructure. The claw pattern is canonical; FFS should be a citizen of it, not a competitor.

### Alternative 2: Build a minimal FFS-specific daemon as the only option

- **Description:** Ship only the minimal-FFS-daemon implementation. Don't support OpenClaw integration.
- **Pros:** Sharper FFS focus. Less dependency on external claw projects.
- **Cons:** Cuts off users who already run OpenClaw and want FFS to run inside it. Doubles the effort to maintain both a daemon and skills versus letting OpenClaw host the skills directly.
- **Why rejected:** The choice is operational. Both paths should be supported; the implementation decides based on practical considerations at build time.

## Consequences

### Positive

- FFS leverages the claw ecosystem (OpenClaw, Hermes, NemoClaw) rather than competing with it.
- Users who already run a claw can install FFS skills into their existing workspace without a separate daemon.
- Multi-channel routing (WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, voice) comes for free via the claw layer.
- The FFS agents are portable across claw implementations because they conform to the `SKILL.md` pattern.

### Negative

- FFS's agent capabilities are constrained by what the chosen claw supports. Custom needs (e.g., FFS-specific resource limits) must be expressed in claw-compatible terms.
- Two integration paths (OpenClaw and minimal-FFS-daemon) means two installation experiences to document and support.

### Risks

- OpenClaw or Hermes pivots in incompatible ways. **Mitigation:** Both are open-source under active community governance. The minimal-FFS-daemon path provides an escape if the claw landscape destabilizes.
- The `SKILL.md` format diverges across claws. **Mitigation:** FFS skills target a common subset; claw-specific extensions are isolated.

## Implementation Notes

An FFS agent definition is a directory containing:

```
ffs-scribe/
├── SKILL.md              # metadata: type, capabilities, schedule, entry points
├── definition.atom.json  # the FFS agent definition atom (signed, versioned)
├── extraction.py         # the actual scribe logic
├── prompts/              # LLM prompts, edition-able
└── tests/                # behavioral tests for this agent's outputs
```

The `SKILL.md` follows OpenClaw's conventions. The `definition.atom.json` is FFS's typed contract — predicate scope, entity scope, capability grants, resource limits, signing key reference. Both files are different views of the same thing.

The MVP daemon implementation choice (OpenClaw or minimal FFS) does not affect the agent definitions; the same skills load into either host.

This ADR replaces the standalone `CLAW.md` document from prior architecture iterations. The claw integration is a single architectural decision, properly scoped here.

## References

- See PRD § Core Features § Daemon.
- See PRD § High-Level Technical Constraints § Required integrations.
- See PRD § Open Questions for the OpenClaw-vs-minimal-daemon implementation choice.
##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-013.md
# ADR-013: MCP server in MVP

## Status

Accepted (supersedes [ADR-010](adr-010.md))

## Date

2026-05-05

## Context

ADR-010 deferred the FFS-MCP server to Phase 2, reasoning that the small-community success criterion is advanced by personal federation rather than by ecosystem-scale MCP integration, and that the CLI plus `ffs://` URL resolution is sufficient developer surface for MVP.

That reasoning underweighted a specific concern. The home-claw absorption scenario is one of the three MVP scenarios (per ADR-004): power users running many AI agents on personal hardware, with agents writing markdown to the substrate for absorption. Writing to ingest via the filesystem is one half of that scenario; reading substrate state via MCP is the other half.

Without an MCP server in MVP:

- AI agents can write markdown to the ingest folder but cannot query the substrate. They cannot ask "what are my recent decisions about the Acme deal?" or "what contacts do I have in tech?" before they generate output.
- The home-claw absorption scenario validates the substrate's *write* path but not its *read* path for MCP-aware agents.
- Developer-audience evaluation depends on the substrate-API or CLI rather than on the standardized agent integration protocol the rest of the ecosystem uses.

The MCP server is also a thin wrapper over the substrate's existing API. The substantial work is the substrate, which MVP ships anyway. Six MCP tools with capability checks at the boundary is on the order of days to weeks of implementation, not months.

## Decision

The FFS-MCP server is MVP, not Phase 2. The MVP server exposes six tools:

- **`ffs_query`** — query the substrate by entity, predicate, or time range; capability-checked.
- **`ffs_render_projection`** — render a projection at a path; equivalent to `ffs cat` over MCP.
- **`ffs_resolve_url`** — resolve an `ffs://` URL.
- **`ffs_author_atom`** — propose an atom into the ingest path with provenance; capability-checked at signing.
- **`ffs_inspect_predicate`** — return a predicate spec so an agent can understand the substrate's vocabulary.
- **`ffs_audit_query`** — run audit queries (recent atoms, supersessions, classifications, capability events).

Capability checks fire at the MCP boundary; an agent receives only what its identity is entitled to. An agent attempting to author an atom outside its capability scope receives a structured error rather than silent failure.

Richer MCP tool surfaces — federation operations, capability authoring via MCP, real-time subscription to atom updates, additional tools the small community asks for — are Phase 2.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Keep MCP server deferred to Phase 2 (the ADR-010 position)

- **Description:** MVP ships the substrate's local API and the `ffs` CLI as developer-audience surfaces. MCP server is Phase 2.
- **Pros:** Smaller MVP scope. Sharper focus on small-community validation. MCP server tool design can be informed by MVP usage.
- **Cons:** Home-claw absorption scenario is half-validated in MVP — agents write but don't read. Developers evaluating FFS see a substrate without the standardized agent-integration protocol the rest of the 2026 ecosystem uses.
- **Why rejected:** The home-claw absorption scenario's full validation requires bidirectional MCP. ADR-010 prioritized adoption-pacing over scenario-completeness; that's the wrong tradeoff for one of MVP's three motivating scenarios.

### Alternative 2: Ship a partial MCP server (e.g., read-only tools)

- **Description:** MVP ships `ffs_query`, `ffs_render_projection`, and `ffs_resolve_url` (the read tools). Defer `ffs_author_atom` and the audit/inspect tools to Phase 2.
- **Pros:** Smaller surface than the full six tools. Read-only is simpler.
- **Cons:** Half-shipping the MCP server creates an awkward middle. Agents that read substrate state may also need to write; cutting `ffs_author_atom` forces them back to filesystem-writes-to-ingest, which works but inconsistently with how they read. Better to ship the coherent six-tool set or keep the deferral.
- **Why rejected:** Coherence over partial delivery. The six tools form a tight set; cutting any of them creates an asymmetry that isn't a meaningful scope reduction.

## Consequences

### Positive

- The home-claw absorption scenario is fully validated in MVP. Agents read substrate state via MCP; agents write to ingest via filesystem; the substrate handles both paths correctly.
- Developers evaluating FFS see the standardized 2026 agent-integration protocol working, not just the CLI.
- The both-audiences-first-class commitment (ADR-002) is honored substantively rather than nominally.
- Phase 2 adds richer MCP tools informed by MVP usage rather than starting MCP integration from scratch in Phase 2.

### Negative

- MVP scope grows. The six MCP tools with capability checks are real implementation work, even as a thin wrapper.
- The MCP server is one more surface to maintain — bug fixes, capability-check correctness, error-message clarity.

### Risks

- The MCP server's tool surface turns out to be wrong for what agents actually need. **Mitigation:** Phase 2 explicitly reserves capacity for richer MCP tools informed by MVP usage. The six tools are the conservative starter set; richer ones come from real demand.
- Capability-check enforcement at the MCP boundary has subtle bugs that allow unauthorized authoring. **Mitigation:** Capability checks are evaluated by the same fixed evaluator that the substrate's local API uses; the MCP server is a thin wrapper that delegates capability evaluation, not a separate enforcement layer.

## Implementation Notes

The MCP server runs alongside the local daemon. Agents connect via the standard MCP transport (stdio or SSE per the agent's configuration). The Obsidian plugin and CLI continue to use the substrate's local API directly; the MCP server is for MCP-aware external agents.

Capability checks delegate to the substrate's existing capability evaluator. The MCP server constructs the same query that the local API would receive, applies the agent's identity, and returns capability-filtered results. There is no parallel capability machinery in the MCP layer.

The six MVP tools are the conservative starter set. Phase 2 adds tools as MVP usage reveals what's needed.

## References

- See PRD § Core Features § FFS-MCP server.
- See PRD § Phased Rollout Plan § MVP.
- See [ADR-002](adr-002.md) (both audiences first-class).
- See [ADR-004](adr-004.md) (three motivating scenarios in MVP).
- See [ADR-008](adr-008.md) (speak MCP and A2A at boundaries).
- See [ADR-010](adr-010.md) (the superseded prior decision).
##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-022.md
# ADR-022: Substrate-is-vault — `$FFS_DATA_DIR` is the Obsidian vault root

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-06-02

## Context

The installer landed in task_22 with a `--vault <path>` flag that accepted any directory and copied the Obsidian plugin into `<vault>/.obsidian/plugins/ffs/`. The materializer (task_25) writes projection files to `$FFS_DATA_DIR/contacts/by-name/...`, `$FFS_DATA_DIR/notes/by-name/...`, etc. When the user passed `--vault /some/other/path`, the materializer wrote into `$FFS_DATA_DIR` (default `~/.ffs/`) and the user's Obsidian vault — which was elsewhere — appeared empty.

This was discovered during the post-task_26 first-use rehearsal: the substrate was working end-to-end, atoms were being signed and materialized, but the user's Obsidian file explorer (rooted at `~/Library/Mobile Documents/iCloud~md~obsidian/Documents/ffs-test/`) had nothing in it because materialized contacts landed at `~/.ffs/contacts/by-name/S/Sara_Chen.md`.

The original PRD and ARCHITECTURE.md always assumed `~/.ffs/` *was* the vault — the path-library structure is opinionated about that. The installer's `--vault` flag was inherited unreflectively from a generic "Obsidian plugin installer" mental model and never reconciled with the substrate's mental model.

## Decision

`$FFS_DATA_DIR` (default `~/.ffs/`) is canonically the Obsidian vault root. The installer seeds `$FFS_DATA_DIR/.obsidian/plugins/ffs/` directly. The user's first-time Obsidian step is **Open folder as vault → `~/.ffs/`** — there is no separate vault to choose or configure.

The installer's `--vault <path>` flag stays accepted for backwards compatibility, but supplying a path different from `$FFS_DATA_DIR` triggers a warning to stderr/stdout explaining that the materializer writes to `$FFS_DATA_DIR` and an external vault will appear empty.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Configurable vault path that the materializer writes to

- **Description:** Make `$FFS_VAULT_DIR` separate from `$FFS_DATA_DIR`. The materializer writes projections to `$FFS_VAULT_DIR/contacts/by-name/...`; substrate state (atoms.db, ingest/, skills/, run/, log/) stays at `$FFS_DATA_DIR`.
- **Pros:** Respects users who already have an Obsidian vault and want to keep using it.
- **Cons:** Doubles the configuration surface. Splits the path-library — `ingest/` lives in one root and `contacts/` lives in another, even though they're conceptually parts of the same substrate. The fast-path watcher (task_09) becomes harder: it needs to watch two roots and reconcile cross-root events. The Obsidian plugin, the CLI, and the federation pull path all need to know the split.
- **Why rejected:** YAGNI. Federation, not iCloud sync or external vaults, is FFS's answer to "use this knowledge from multiple devices."

### Alternative 2: Symlink-based externalization

- **Description:** `$FFS_DATA_DIR` stays the single substrate root, but the installer can symlink `<external-vault>/contacts → ~/.ffs/contacts`, same for `ingest/`, `notes/`, etc.
- **Pros:** Substrate stays unified; the user can keep their existing vault.
- **Cons:** Symlinks are fragile across platforms (iCloud sync resolves them inconsistently; Windows handles them differently; future federation pulls may walk through them in unexpected ways). The fast-path watcher's canonicalization (`std::fs::canonicalize`) already had to be added for `notify::PollWatcher` on macOS; symlinks would compound that.
- **Why rejected:** Real symlink semantics across three OSes is a maintenance liability that doesn't earn its place in MVP.

### Alternative 3: Status quo — installer requires explicit `--vault`

- **Description:** Keep the original task_22 design. User picks a vault path explicitly; installer warns when omitted; user is responsible for understanding that the vault path and the substrate path must match.
- **Pros:** No code changes.
- **Cons:** The user IS the one who hit the failure mode that prompted this ADR — the architecture didn't surface the constraint until it broke their experience. "User responsible for understanding" isn't a design; it's an admission that the design hasn't decided.
- **Why rejected:** The first-use rehearsal proved the failure mode is too easy to fall into. Picking a sensible default removes the trap.

## Consequences

### Positive

- One root path, one mental model: "FFS owns `~/.ffs/`. To use it, open `~/.ffs/` in Obsidian."
- The installer Just Works with no `--vault` argument — the friction floor for technical-friend onboarding drops by one decision.
- The materializer's path resolution, the fast-path watcher's root, and the Obsidian plugin's expected vault all point at the same directory. No cross-root reconciliation logic.
- `~/.ffs/` is not iCloud-synced by default (it lives directly under `$HOME`), which sidesteps the FS-watcher-vs-cloud-sync friction the troubleshooting guide already warns about. Federation handles cross-device data movement more cleanly than iCloud sync would, since FFS atoms are signed and content-addressed.

### Negative

- Users with strong "I already have an Obsidian vault and want FFS to live inside it" preferences must either (a) accept the warning when they pass `--vault`, or (b) wait for a future symlink-or-mirror feature (out of MVP scope).
- The `~/.ffs/.obsidian/` directory now contains Obsidian's per-vault state (workspace.json, etc.) alongside the substrate. It's organizationally clean — the `.obsidian/` directory is owned by Obsidian, and the substrate ignores it — but it adds visible structure under `~/.ffs/` that previously wasn't there.

### Risks

- **A user who runs the installer with an explicit `--vault` may not notice the warning** and end up with an empty external vault while their substrate populates `~/.ffs/`. **Mitigation**: the warning is repeated three times in the installer output (`WARN` lines on consecutive lines), the troubleshooting guide gets an explicit entry for it, and the post-task_30 docs no longer mention `--vault` outside of the migration section.

## Implementation Notes

- `installer/install.sh::install_obsidian_plugin()` defaults `VAULT_PATH="$DATA_DIR"` when the flag is unset.
- `installer/install.ps1` does the same for Windows.
- The `installer_layout` regression test (`crates/ffs-daemon/tests/installer_layout.rs`) covers the new layout: no `--vault`, `--vault $FFS_DATA_DIR`, and `--vault /external/path` all produce the right files in the right places (or warn, in the external case).
- `docs/onboarding/first-use-guide.md` opens with "Step 0: open `~/.ffs/` as your Obsidian vault."
- `docs/onboarding/technical-friend-checklist.md` includes a migration section for users who installed before this change.

## References

- [ADR-005: Editor-agnostic working set materialization](adr-005.md) — Real files on disk for any editor; this ADR clarifies *which* directory holds them.
- [ADR-011: Path library starts at three (contacts/people/notes)](adr-011.md) — The path-library layout is rooted at the substrate root, which is now also the vault root.
- task_22 (installer scripts) — Original `--vault` behavior being reshaped.
- task_25 (working-set materializer) — Always wrote to `$FFS_DATA_DIR`, never anywhere else.
- task_26 first-use rehearsal — Where the gap was discovered.
##### .compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/adrs/adr-023.md
# ADR-023: Code-signed macOS binaries with shared `keychain-access-group`

## Status

Accepted (intent) — **Implementation specifics superseded by [ADR-025](adr-025.md)**.

Empirical investigation during task_35 (2026-06-19) proved that
the section-embed mechanism this ADR prescribed — wiring the
provisioning profile into the Mach-O via
`-Wl,-sectcreate,__TEXT,__provisioning,…` — is folklore. AMFI
never reads that section; the profile has to be a file at
`Contents/embedded.provisionprofile` inside a `.app` bundle. The
**intent** of this ADR (Apple-issued code signing + the shared
`3S9R9K2L38.com.ffs.shared` access group + notarization for
distribution trust) stays correct and is upheld. The
**implementation** (how the provisioning profile gets to AMFI) is
corrected by ADR-025.

## Date

2026-06-13 (intent); implementation correction landed via ADR-025 on 2026-06-19.

## Context

Task_27 added the macOS Keychain integration: helper functions in `ffs-core::store::keyring` that wrap the `keyring` v3 crate, plus a daemon-side precedence chain (env-var → keychain → generate-and-warn). Unit tests passed; the `FFS_KEYRING_DISABLE` integration test passed. But the first live launchd deploy revealed three distinct daemon identities across three consecutive launchd-triggered boots:

```
boot 1 (launchd): owner=z3MD…  source=keychain
boot 2 (launchd): owner=zEoA…  source=keychain   ← different!
CLI (interactive): owner=zEXqe… source=keychain   ← also different!
```

Each boot wrote a fresh "keychain entry" that the next boot couldn't see, so each boot generated a new key, broke the SQLCipher DEK match against the existing `atoms.db`, and crashed.

Two compounding root causes:

1. **The keyring crate wasn't actually hitting macOS Keychain Services.** The workspace `Cargo.toml` declared `keyring = "3"` without specifying features. keyring v3 has *no default features*; on macOS without `apple-native` it silently falls back to its `mock` backend (an in-process HashMap that disappears on process exit). Every boot wrote to a fresh mock and "read" nothing on the next boot.

2. **Even with `apple-native` enabled, keyring v3 doesn't pass `kSecAttrAccessGroup`.** Its macOS backend calls `find_generic_password` / `set_generic_password` from `security-framework` without supplying an access group. Apple Keychain Services partitions generic-password entries by the writing binary's *code-signing identity* AND its *launch context*. So even after fixing the first bug, the launchd-spawned daemon (no terminal, runs as a daemon process) would not see entries written by the interactively-spawned CLI (terminal-attached, runs as a user process). Different launch contexts ⇒ different keychain partitions ⇒ same code, same binary, but invisible writes.

The fix is to (a) actually use the real macOS keychain backend, and (b) place every FFS binary in a shared, explicitly-named keychain access group so the partitioning doesn't matter.

## Decision

FFS adopts a **two-part fix**:

1. **Enable `keyring` v3's `apple-native` feature** on the workspace dep so the macOS backend actually reaches `Security/Security.h` instead of the mock. Also enable the equivalent native backends for Linux (`linux-native-sync-persistent`) and Windows (`windows-native`) so the crate's behavior is consistent across the matrix.

2. **Drop down to `security-framework` directly on macOS** in `ffs-core::store::keyring_macos`, calling `set_generic_password_options` / `generic_password` with an explicit `kSecAttrAccessGroup`. The access group is `3S9R9K2L38.com.ffs.shared` (project lead's Apple Developer Team ID + project namespace).

3. **Codesign every FFS binary** (`ffs`, `ffs-daemon`, `ffs-mcp`) with an `entitlements/ffs.entitlements.plist` declaring `keychain-access-groups = [3S9R9K2L38.com.ffs.shared]`. `scripts/codesign-macos.sh` is the local-dev tool; the GitHub Actions release workflow does the same with secrets-fed identity.

4. **Gate the keychain path on signed-binary detection at startup**. The daemon shells out to `codesign -d --entitlements - <self>` and looks for the access-group string in the output. When the running binary lacks the entitlement (unsigned dev build, missing Developer ID), the daemon logs a one-time warning and routes the keychain helpers down the same "disabled" path that `FFS_KEYRING_DISABLE=1` triggers — keeps the dev loop fast and avoids the cross-process chaos task_27's first deploy hit.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1 — Keep keyring v3 + accept partitioned writes

- **Description:** Enable `apple-native` only; don't set an access group; accept that the daemon and CLI see different entries.
- **Pros:** Smallest change. No `security-framework` direct dep.
- **Cons:** Doesn't actually solve the problem. The daemon would still generate a new key on every launchd boot and the substrate would still be unusable.
- **Why rejected:** Punts the bug.

### Alternative 2 — File-based shared secret instead of keychain

- **Description:** Skip the keychain entirely. Write the owner-key seed and DEK to `$FFS_DATA_DIR/run/keystore.json` mode `0600`.
- **Pros:** No keychain plumbing, no signing requirement, works everywhere identically.
- **Cons:** The whole point of the keychain integration is to put the secrets *somewhere other than disk*, where a file-system backup, accidental sync to a cloud drive, or git mishap can't carry them off. The Unix `chmod 0600` only protects against other local users; the keychain protects against the user's own missteps too. The PRD's "this is records about my life" framing means the user is going to back up `$FFS_DATA_DIR`; the keychain belongs outside that backup boundary.
- **Why rejected:** Defeats the security goal task_27 was scoped to meet.

### Alternative 3 — Submit a keyring v3 patch upstream

- **Description:** Add `with_access_group(group)` to `keyring::Entry` in the upstream crate, then use that from `ffs-core`.
- **Pros:** Doesn't fork the dep landscape. Other projects with the same need would benefit.
- **Cons:** Upstream timeline is unbounded. The FFS critical path (task_27 unblock) can't wait. Even if the patch lands quickly, the new API would be on a future minor version we'd have to wait to use.
- **Why rejected:** Time horizon. Worth doing as a parallel upstream contribution, but not as the FFS unblock.

## Consequences

### Positive

- The launchd-vs-interactive partitioning problem stops mattering: both contexts read the same access-group bucket.
- Signed-binary detection means the unsigned dev loop (running `cargo run`) keeps working without keychain entanglement — the gate logs a clear pointer to `scripts/codesign-macos.sh` and falls through to the env-var / generate path.
- The CI release workflow produces signed `.tar.gz` artifacts when the three signing secrets are configured. Forks without those secrets still get builds; they just get unsigned binaries that follow the env-var-or-generate fallback.

### Negative

- New runtime dep on `codesign` (a stock macOS tool — present on every macOS install with Command Line Tools). Without it, `is_signed_with_keychain_entitlement` returns false and the keychain path stays off.
- The signing requirement raises the floor for "production-shaped macOS install." A user building locally must either run `scripts/codesign-macos.sh` after `cargo build --release` or accept the unsigned/env-var path. The technical-friend-checklist now documents both routes.
- `security-framework` is added as a direct macOS-only dep on `ffs-core`. It was already a transitive dep via `keyring`'s `apple-native` feature; the direct add is small but it does increase the macOS build surface.

### Risks

- **Apple keychain partitioning rules change.** Apple occasionally tightens what entitlements a binary needs to read its own writes. The `keychain-access-groups` mechanism has been stable since macOS 10.10, but Apple's behavior under hardened runtime + notarization is an evolving target. **Mitigation:** the daemon's gate fails open to env-var, so a future Apple-side surprise produces a clear log message rather than data loss.
- **Notarization adds extra steps for distribution.** Codesigning is necessary but not sufficient for Gatekeeper to admit a downloaded `.dmg` past macOS 10.15. Notarization is not in this ADR's scope; it's a follow-up when FFS ships a public `.dmg`. The `--options runtime` flag in the codesign script is the hardened-runtime opt-in that notarization will require.

## Implementation Notes

The `keychain-access-groups` value must use the *project-namespaced* form `<TeamID>.<group>`. Apple uses that prefix to ensure groups are unique across developers — without it the codesign step fails with "access group is not in entitlements" or similar.

The runtime detection helper looks at the **merged stdout + stderr** of `codesign -d --entitlements - --xml`. Some macOS versions route the entitlement payload to stderr instead of stdout; we treat any substring match as a positive ID.

The daemon's `keychain_path_enabled()` composite check is `!FFS_KEYRING_DISABLE && is_signed_with_keychain_entitlement()`. The env-var path takes priority because tests need to be able to skip the keychain even on a signed binary.

### AMFI requires an embedded provisioning profile, not just signing

The above is necessary but not sufficient. Empirical finding (2026-06-14, macOS 26.2): a Developer-ID-signed, notarized, hardened-runtime, entitled binary that **doesn't carry an embedded provisioning profile** is silently `SIGKILL`ed by AMFI (kernel-level Apple Mobile File Integrity) before `main()` runs. Exit code 137. Zero stderr. No log entries the unprivileged side can see. Strip the entitlement → the same binary launches normally.

`keychain-access-groups` is a **restricted** entitlement (per [Apple TN3125](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3125-inside-code-signing-provisioning-profiles)). Restricted entitlements have to be allowlisted by either Apple's own signing authority (App Store path — not us) or an **embedded provisioning profile** whose entitlements dict matches the binary's claims. AMFI verifies this at exec; mismatch → `EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL)`, before any user code runs.

Quinn "Eskimo" Apple DTS in [thread/685723](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/685723):

> "Other entitlements must be allowlisted by a provisioning profile, just like on iOS… the fact that the keychain-access-groups entitlement must be allowlisted by a profile means that other developers can't impersonate your app to steal its keychain items."

There is no `--preserve-metadata` / `--deep` workaround. The single supported path is to embed the profile.

### Provisioning profile lifecycle for Developer ID CLI binaries

Apple's portal now hides the old "Keychain Sharing" capability toggle on the App ID page — Eskimo, [thread/782084](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/782084), "every App ID automatically gains the Keychain Access capability… there is no Keychain Sharing capability because there's nothing for it to do." Authorization happens via the profile, not via App ID capabilities. The provisioning steps:

1. **App ID** at `developer.apple.com` → Identifiers → "+" → App IDs → App. Bundle ID `com.fornado.ffs` (or any bundle ID owned by team `3S9R9K2L38`). No capability checkboxes need to be touched.
2. **Profile** at `developer.apple.com` → Profiles → "+" → **Distribution** section → **Developer ID** → select the App ID + the Developer ID Application cert. Download → save as `embedded.provisionprofile`.
3. **Embed at build time.** Apple's documented path for non-`.app` Mach-O binaries is the linker section `__TEXT,__provisioning`, populated via `ld -sectcreate __TEXT __provisioning embedded.provisionprofile` ([Eskimo, thread/657917](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/657917)). For Rust, each binary crate has a `build.rs` that emits:
   ```rust
   println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-Wl,-sectcreate,__TEXT,__provisioning,<path>");
   ```
   when `FFS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` is set. Builds without the env var are no-ops; cross-OS builds don't care.

`scripts/codesign-macos.sh` refuses to sign a binary that lacks the `__TEXT,__provisioning` section — surfaces the configuration error at sign time instead of letting it manifest as an inscrutable runtime SIGKILL.

### CI integration test path (skip-when-unsigned)

The integration test (`signed_daemon_produces_stable_keychain_identity_across_boots` in `tests/sqlite_persistence.rs`) honors an `FFS_SIGNED_DAEMON_BIN` env var pointing at a pre-built, pre-signed daemon binary. cargo / nextest rebuild the test-build daemon every test run and re-`adhoc`-sign it, blasting any Developer ID signature off — so the test can't use `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_ffs-daemon")` for the signed scenario. The recommended local invocation:

```sh
FFS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE="$PWD/secrets/embedded.provisionprofile" \
  cargo build --release
./scripts/codesign-macos.sh \
  target/release/ffs target/release/ffs-daemon target/release/ffs-mcp
# notarize via `xcrun notarytool submit … --wait`
export FFS_SIGNING_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: …"
export FFS_SIGNED_DAEMON_BIN="$PWD/target/release/ffs-daemon"
cargo nextest run -p ffs-daemon --test sqlite_persistence \
  signed_daemon_produces_stable_keychain_identity_across_boots
```

Without `FFS_SIGNED_DAEMON_BIN`, the test falls through to `CARGO_BIN_EXE_ffs-daemon` (the cargo-managed adhoc-signed binary) and skips with `eprintln!` when `FFS_SIGNING_IDENTITY` is also unset. Contributor PRs without an Apple Developer Program enrollment keep CI green.

### Defense-in-depth on the .p12 password

Initial draft (commit `edaa2cf`) stored the throwaway `.p12` password on disk in `secrets/p12.password` alongside the `.p12` itself. Subsequent revision removed it: defense-in-depth says two secrets in one place is one secret. The `.p12` stays in `secrets/` as an emergency restore; the password lives only in the user's password manager + the `MACOS_SIGNING_CERT_PASSWORD` GitHub Actions secret.

## References (additional, beyond §6)

# ADR-024: Windows ACL hardening at install time via `icacls`, not in the daemon

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-06-11

## Context

The Unix daemon binary applies `chmod 0o700` to `$FFS_DATA_DIR/run/` at startup (`crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs`) so a malicious local process can't swap the UDS file out from under us between bind and accept. That's a defense-in-depth check sitting on top of the OS's per-user home-directory protections.

Windows has no `chmod`. The closest equivalent is to write a DACL granting Full Control to the current user and nothing to anyone else. Two implementation sites were considered for task_34:

- **Option A — daemon-side.** Call `SetNamedSecurityInfoW` from `crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs` via `windows-sys`. Pros: enforcement runs every daemon boot, even if the user side-stepped the installer. Cons: pulls a large platform crate into the daemon for what is effectively a setup-time concern; the ACL code lives in main.rs forever and needs to be maintained alongside the Unix path.

- **Option B — installer-side.** Have `installer/install.ps1` invoke `icacls` once at install time to lock down `$FFS_DATA_DIR` (and its `run/` subdirectory) to the current user. Pros: matches the Unix story exactly (the *installer* runs `chmod 0o700`, not the daemon — `installer/install.sh` already does this). Keeps the daemon binary platform-agnostic. Cons: someone who deletes the ACL between install and boot gets an unhardened directory until the next install.

## Decision

Task_34 uses **Option B (installer-side `icacls`)**.

`installer/install.ps1` invokes `icacls "$DataDir" /inheritance:r /grant:r "$env:USERNAME:(OI)(CI)F"` on the data root and the `run/` subdirectory after creating them. The daemon's `main.rs` leaves the existing `#[cfg(unix)]` `chmod 0o700` block alone and adds no Windows counterpart.

## Alternatives Considered

### Option A — daemon-side `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`

- **Description:** The daemon binary calls `windows-sys` ACL APIs to harden `$FFS_DATA_DIR/run/` at every startup.
- **Pros:** Re-enforces hardening on every boot. Survives an ACL deletion between install and boot.
- **Cons:** Adds a meaningful Windows-only dependency (`windows-sys` Win32::Security feature set, ~300 KB of generated bindings) to the daemon binary for what is fundamentally a setup-time concern. Asymmetric with the Unix story where the chmod lives in the *installer*, not the daemon — Unix's `installer/install.sh` already does `chmod 0o700 "$DATA_DIR"`. The daemon-side Unix chmod at `main.rs:135` is an additional belt-and-braces guard specifically on the socket's parent dir, not the data dir.
- **Why rejected:** The dep-weight + complexity asymmetry isn't worth re-enforcement on every boot. A user who manually clears the ACL has bigger problems and will see the next install fix it.

### Option C — neither (rely on `$LOCALAPPDATA` / `$USERPROFILE` defaults)

- **Description:** Skip explicit ACL hardening; trust that Windows' default ACL on `%USERPROFILE%\.ffs\` (inherited from the user profile) already restricts to the current user.
- **Pros:** Zero installer code, zero daemon code, no platform deps.
- **Cons:** Default ACLs on `%USERPROFILE%` may inherit broader rights from parent folders depending on Group Policy / domain configuration / OEM image. Defense-in-depth is exactly the place to not rely on environmental defaults — that's why the Unix daemon does `chmod 0o700` *on top of* the home-directory default.
- **Why rejected:** Equivalent posture to the Unix story is the goal; "trust the default" doesn't meet it.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Daemon binary stays platform-agnostic. No `windows-sys` dep, no `#[cfg(windows)]` ACL block in `main.rs`.
- Story matches Unix: the installer hardens the data dir; the daemon trusts that hardening at runtime.
- `icacls` is a stock Windows command — no PowerShell module dependency, works on every supported Windows since 7.

### Negative

- An adversary who clears the ACL between install and daemon boot gets an unhardened state until the next install runs. The mitigation is "users who alter their data dir's ACL get what they ask for."

### Risks

- **`icacls` semantics edge cases.** `icacls` flag combinations are notoriously fiddly; the chosen `/inheritance:r /grant:r "<user>:(OI)(CI)F"` form has the specific effect of "remove inherited permissions, grant the current user Full Control with Object Inherit + Container Inherit." Verified via the `icacls "$Dir"` output post-install — the install.ps1 step is followed by a verification call.
- **Service vs. interactive identity.** If the user later registers the daemon as a Windows service rather than the at-logon scheduled task that install.ps1 wires up, the running identity differs from `$env:USERNAME`. That's out of scope for MVP (the installer uses the scheduled-task path) but should be revisited if a service installer lands.

## Implementation Notes

The `icacls` invocation lives in `installer/install.ps1`:

```powershell
function Harden-Acl($path) {
    if ($DryRun) {
        Write-Host "+ icacls $path /inheritance:r /grant:r `"$env:USERNAME`":(OI)(CI)F"
    } else {
        & icacls $path /inheritance:r /grant:r "$($env:USERNAME):(OI)(CI)F" | Out-Null
    }
}

Harden-Acl $DataDir
Harden-Acl (Join-Path $DataDir 'run')
```

The flags decompose as:

- `/inheritance:r` — remove inherited ACEs from the target. Without this, ACEs from `$env:USERPROFILE` (or further up if domain-joined) propagate.
- `/grant:r "user:(OI)(CI)F"` — replace any existing ACE for `user` with `Full Control`, applied to this folder, subfolders (Container Inherit), and files within (Object Inherit).

## References

- See `installer/install.sh` for the Unix sibling that does `chmod 0o700 "$DATA_DIR"`.
- See `crates/ffs-daemon/src/main.rs` for the daemon-side `chmod 0o700` on `run/` (Unix-only).
- See task_34 for the broader Windows daemon-path correctness work that this ADR is a piece of.
- Microsoft documentation: `icacls` flag reference — `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/icacls`.

# ADR-026: Scribe v2 — predicate-schema-driven extraction with pluggable engines

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-06-21

## Context

The scribe skill (task_11, refined in task_32) extracts structured proposals from free-text notes dropped into `ingest/`. Its extraction logic is regex heuristics: a `[A-Z][a-z]+\s+[A-Z][a-z]+` bigram scan for names, pattern detectors for phones/emails, a stop-word list, venue masking. Live use on 2026-06-21 produced the canonical failure: a file named `Jon Jones.md` containing a key-value contact card (`Nickname: Bones / Occupation: UFC fighter / Phone numbe r- 9194284074`) was extracted as a `contact.person` with **`display_name: "Bones Occupation"`** — two random title-case words stitched across lines. Five distinct failure modes were catalogued (filename ignored, key-value card shape unrecognized, field labels treated as name candidates, no cross-check against the filename, verbatim typo propagation).

The deeper diagnosis: **this is not a regex-quality problem, it is an architecture problem.** Two structural facts make the current design wrong regardless of how clever the patterns get:

1. **Scribe ignores the predicate registry.** FFS predicates are defined in TOML specs carrying real JSON Schemas (`claim_schema` blocks) — the substrate already knows, in machine-readable form, exactly what shapes it can hold. The scribe hardcodes `contact.person` and `note` logic instead of consuming those schemas. Every new predicate the user registers is invisible to extraction until someone hand-writes new regexes.
2. **The quality ceiling of pattern-matching is far below what the substrate needs.** "Records-shaped substrate for personal knowledge" is the project thesis; the scribe is the front door through which records enter. A front door that guesses names from capitalized bigrams caps the entire system's usefulness.

The decision below resolves a question that blocked progress for roughly two months: which extraction technology, given the tension between quality (frontier LLM APIs), privacy (personal records leaving the machine), and operational weight (local model installs). The resolution came from noticing that **four of the five blocking sub-questions answer themselves from constraints already committed in this repository**:

| Blocking question | Answer, and where it was already decided |
|---|---|
| Is "records never leave the machine" a hard line? | Wrong framing. The distinction that matters is **ambient vs. invoked**. The substrate is SQLCipher-encrypted and local-first, but `ffs-mcp` (task_16) exists precisely so Claude can read the substrate when the user invokes it. A daemon that silently ships every note to an API is ambient exfiltration; a user-configured engine choice is invocation. Resolution: **local-only default, cloud backend as explicit opt-in configuration.** The blocker dissolves from a decision into a setting. |
| Extraction scope — contacts, or everything? | The predicate registry answers this. Extraction must target **whatever predicates are registered**, driven by their `claim_schema`s. Hardcoding any predicate shape is the bug being fixed, not a scope option. |
| Latency budget? | Non-issue. The ingest stability window (task_31, 30 s) plus the asynchronous quarantine mean extraction latency is invisible below ~30 s. Quality wins every latency tradeoff available. |
| Acceptable dependencies? | ADR-009 is decisive: skill bundles are **stdlib-only, zero pip dependencies**. This *eliminates* classical NER (spaCy/GLiNER require torch) and *selects* LLM-over-HTTP: both the Anthropic Messages API and a localhost Ollama server are plain JSON-over-HTTP, callable with `urllib.request` from the standard library. Python 3.11+ `tomllib` likewise reads the predicate TOMLs with zero deps. |
| Feedback/correction loop? | Already exists — the quarantine's accept/reject flow (tasks 19, 29). Record which engine+model produced each proposal in provenance; defer fine-tuning on accept/reject history to post-MVP. |

## Decision

Scribe v2 restructures extraction around two seams:

**1. Engine abstraction.** An `ExtractionEngine` interface inside the skill bundle (stdlib-only Python), with two implementations:

- **`heuristic`** — today's regex code, refactored behind the interface. Always available, fully offline, zero configuration. **Remains the default.**
- **`llm`** — a stdlib-`urllib` HTTP client with two thin backend adapters:
  - **Ollama** (`http://localhost:11434/api/chat`) — local models, nothing leaves the machine; for users who install Ollama.
  - **Anthropic Messages API** (`https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`) — highest quality ceiling; explicit opt-in; API key via environment or OS keychain.

  Selection via `FFS_SCRIBE_ENGINE` (`heuristic` | `llm`), backend via `FFS_SCRIBE_LLM_URL` + `FFS_SCRIBE_LLM_MODEL`. Any `llm` failure (network down, malformed output, schema-invalid JSON) falls back to `heuristic` so ingest never hard-fails on connectivity.

**2. Predicate-schema-driven prompts.** The extraction prompt is **generated from the registered predicate specs** — the skill reads the TOMLs from `$FFS_DATA_DIR/config/predicates/` via stdlib `tomllib` and renders each predicate's name, `claim_schema`, and description into the instruction. LLM output is validated against the same `claim_schema` before becoming a proposal. Consequences: adding a predicate extends extraction automatically; the schema is enforced at both ends; the heuristic engine remains the only place with per-predicate hand-written logic (and only as fallback).

Supporting decisions:

- **Provenance** on every proposal gains `engine` + `model` fields, surfaced in the quarantine review UI so the user can calibrate trust per engine.
- **A golden-corpus evaluation harness** (~20 fixture notes including the Jon Jones card, each with expected proposals) scores engines objectively via pytest. Heuristic-engine scores gate CI; LLM-engine scoring runs out-of-band (requires network/models). This converts "the scribe guessed wrong again" into a measured, regression-tested engineering surface.
- **The quarantine remains the human gate.** No proposal commits without user accept, regardless of engine.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Keep improving the heuristics (regex++)

- **Description:** Add filename consultation, key-value card detection, extended stop-lists, cross-checks — the five fixes catalogued from the Jon Jones failure.
- **Pros:** No new moving parts; fully offline; each fix is small.
- **Cons:** Two months of this produced "Bones Occupation." The ceiling is structurally low: every new note shape needs a new hand-written rule, and the registry-blindness is untouched. This is the bandaid path.
- **Why rejected as the strategy:** Retained only as (a) the default/fallback engine and (b) a bounded hygiene pass, because the heuristic engine still serves offline users. Rejected as the answer to extraction quality.

### Alternative 2: Classical NER (spaCy `en_core_web_trf`, GLiNER, NuExtract)

- **Description:** Pretrained token-classification models; ~92% F1 on standard entity types; ~100 ms on Apple Silicon; fully local.
- **Pros:** Fast, private, well-understood.
- **Cons:** **Violates ADR-009** — these require torch-class pip dependencies inside the skill bundle, or a sidecar model-server that is its own operational burden. Also structurally narrower than the requirement: NER tags entity spans; it does not fill arbitrary registered `claim_schema`s.
- **Why rejected:** The ADR-009 constraint alone is disqualifying; the scope mismatch seconds it.

### Alternative 3: Local LLM as the only engine (mandatory Ollama)

- **Description:** Require Ollama + a 5–15 GB model (e.g., Qwen 2.5 7B) on every install; all extraction runs locally through it.
- **Pros:** High quality and private, no cloud dependency.
- **Cons:** Forces a heavyweight install on every user of what is meant to be a light, technical-friend-installable substrate (ADR-005's friction-floor argument). Model supervision (updates, disk, RAM) becomes FFS's problem.
- **Why rejected as mandatory:** Accepted instead as one *backend* of the `llm` engine for users who choose it.

### Alternative 4: Cloud LLM as the only engine (Anthropic-only)

- **Description:** All extraction goes through the Anthropic API.
- **Pros:** Highest accuracy; simplest single path; the user already trusts Anthropic tooling with this repository.
- **Cons:** Ambient transmission of personal records to a third party as a *side effect of dropping a file in a folder* contradicts the local-first, encrypted-at-rest posture the whole substrate is built on. Also fails offline.
- **Why rejected as default:** Accepted as the opt-in backend with the strongest quality ceiling; rejected as ambient default.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Extraction quality ceiling moves from "regex bigram guessing" to "frontier LLM with schema-enforced output," at the user's chosen privacy level.
- The predicate registry becomes the single source of truth for extractable shapes — registering a predicate extends capture automatically.
- The eval corpus makes extraction quality measurable and regression-gated for the first time.
- ADR-009 is preserved: everything is stdlib (`urllib`, `json`, `tomllib`); no pip deps enter the bundle.
- Offline behavior is never worse than today (heuristic fallback on every `llm` failure).

### Negative

- Two engines to maintain; the heuristic engine cannot be deleted.
- LLM extraction is nondeterministic; the eval harness must score semantically (field-level comparisons with tolerance), not byte-exact.
- Prompt rendering from `claim_schema` couples prompt quality to schema quality — poorly-described predicates will extract poorly. (Arguably a feature: it pressures schema hygiene.)
- API-key handling adds a small secrets surface (mitigated: reuse the task_27/33 keychain machinery).

### Risks

- **Small local models may hallucinate fields.** Mitigation: schema validation rejects nonconforming output → heuristic fallback; quarantine catches the rest; eval corpus quantifies per-model reliability before recommending any model.
- **Anthropic API shape drift.** Mitigation: the adapter is ~50 lines of stdlib HTTP; version pinned via `anthropic-version` header; failures degrade to heuristic, never to ingest breakage.

## Implementation Notes

Implementation is scoped in task_36. Key mechanics settled here:

- Skill reads predicate TOMLs directly from `$FFS_DATA_DIR/config/predicates/` (stdlib `tomllib`) rather than extending the skills-host protocol — no daemon changes needed for schema access.
- Engine + backend config flows as environment variables through the existing daemon → skills-host → subprocess env path.
- Heuristic hygiene fixes from the Jon Jones postmortem (filename as name source, `^[A-Z][a-z]+:\s` card-shape detection, field-label stop-words) land as a bounded subtask because the heuristic remains the default engine — explicitly bounded so bandaiding ends here.

## References

- ADR-009 — skill bundles as claw-shaped, stdlib-only artifacts (the constraint that selected the design).
- ADR-005 — friction floor / technical-friend installability (why mandatory Ollama was rejected).
- task_11, task_26, task_32 — the scribe lineage this supersedes in approach.
- task_16 — `ffs-mcp`, the precedent for invoked (not ambient) Claude access to the substrate.
- task_31 — ingest stability window (why latency is a non-issue).
- task_36 — the implementation task carrying this decision.
- 2026-06-21 "Jon Jones / Bones Occupation" failure postmortem — recorded in task_36's Overview.

# Discovery & Exploration Guide Persistent memory is only useful if agents read existing knowledge before acting. This guide explains how to discover, search, and navigate an OKF v0.2 knowledge bundle efficiently without overflowing context windows. --- ## 1. Core Principle: Read Before Write Before writing code, making architectural choices, or adding new memory concepts: 1. **Search existing memory**: Always query the knowledge base first. 2. **Reuse & Extend**: If a concept already covers the topic, update it instead of creating duplicates. 3. **Verify Context**: Inspect existing constraints, requirements, and past decisions. ```mermaid flowchart TD Task["Incoming Task"] --> Search["Search Knowledge
okf_search / okf search"] Search --> Match{"Matching Concept
Found?"} Match -- Yes --> Inspect["Inspect Details
okf_show / okf show"] Inspect --> Update["Update Existing Concept
okf_update / okf update"] Match -- No --> Create["Create New Concept
okf_create / okf create"] Update -.-> Relate["Link Related Concepts
okf_relate / okf relate"] Create -.-> Relate ``` --- ## 2. Progressive Disclosure Pattern To prevent blowing up the LLM context window with large repositories, follow the **Progressive Disclosure** pattern: ```mermaid flowchart TD L1["Level 1: Bundle Root
knowledge/index.md + log.md
Scope & recent changes"] L2["Level 2: Fast Search
okf_search / okf search
BM25 keyword/relevance match"] L3["Level 3: Concept Inspection
okf_show / okf show
Frontmatter, body & direct links"] L4["Level 4: Graph Traversal
Follow links only when deeper context is required"] L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 ``` ### Context Rules & Negative Constraints - **NO Blanket Scans**: Never run `list_dir`, `grep_search`, or `view_file` over the entire `knowledge/` folder. - **Prefer Native MCP Tools**: Use `okf_search` and `okf_show` if available. Common Domain-Neutral Relationship Patterns | Domain | Source Concept | Target Concept | Relationship Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Software** | `decisions/adr-001` | `architecture/database` | *"implements PostgreSQL with connection pooling"* | | **Software** | `bugs/conn-leak` | `architecture/database` | *"affects connection pool eviction logic"* | | **Software** | `research/grpc-benchmarks` | `decisions/adr-002` | *"justifies gRPC over REST for microservices"* | | **Coaching** | `sessions/2026-09-02` | `clients/jane-doe` | *"coaching session with Jane Doe"* | | **Coaching** | `goals/public-speaking` | `clients/jane-doe` | *"target milestone for Jane Doe"* | | **Literature** | `reviews/thinking-fast` | `books/thinking-fast-and-slow` | *"critical review and chapter notes"* | | **Literature** | `books/thinking-fast-and-slow`| `topics/cognitive-biases` | *"explores heuristic decision-making"* | --- ## 3. Creating Relationships with Tooling Use `okf_relate` (MCP) or `okf relate` (CLI) to link two concepts deterministically with automatic frontmatter and markdown updates: #### Option A: Native MCP Tool (Preferred) ```json // Tool: okf_relate { "source_id": "decisions/adr-001", "target_id": "architecture/database", "description": "implements connection pooling strategy" } ``` #### Option B: CLI Fallback ```bash # Agent JSON mode okf relate decisions/adr-001 architecture/database knowledge \ --desc "implements connection pooling strategy" \ --json # Human-readable relate okf relate decisions/adr-001 architecture/database knowledge \ --desc "implements connection pooling strategy" ``` **JSON Output Example**: ```json { "status": "related", "source": "decisions/adr-001", "target": "architecture/database", "description": "implements connection pooling strategy", "updated_files": [ "knowledge/decisions/adr-001.md" ] } ``` --- ## 4. Graph Integrity & Validation Whenever links are added or removed: 1. **Check for Broken Links**: Every link target must resolve to a valid concept path or ID within the bundle. 2. **Check for Orphaned Concepts**: Ensure key concepts are reachable from index files or related concepts. 3. **Run Strict Validation**: - Native MCP Tool: `okf_validate(strict=true)` - CLI Fallback: `okf validate knowledge --strict` Strict validation ensures: - 0 broken links / dangling pointers - 0 orphaned concepts - 0 schema or frontmatter errors

107:## MCP agents
109:FFS ships `ffs-mcp`, a Model Context Protocol server that any MCP-aware agent (Claude Code, ChatGPT desktop, framework-agnostic agents) can spawn as a subprocess. It exposes six tools, each translating to a daemon JSON-RPC call with capability checks at the daemon boundary:
120:Sample Claude Code `mcpServers` block:
124:  "mcpServers": {
126:      "command": "ffs-mcp",
137:Per ADR-013, capability checks live on the daemon side; the MCP server is a thin pass-through. A capability denial comes back as an MCP tool-level error (`isError: true`) with the typed reason in `details.kind`, not a JSON-RPC error — so the agent surfaces "the substrate refused this" cleanly without treating it as a transport break.
=====
Sample Claude Code `mcpServers` block:

```jsonc
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ffs": {
      "command": "ffs-mcp",
      "args": [],
      "env": {
        "FFS_DAEMON_SOCKET": "/Users/you/.ffs/run/ffs.sock",
        "FFS_AGENT_KEY": "/Users/you/.ffs/keys/claude.ed25519"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Per ADR-013, capability checks live on the daemon side; the MCP server is a thin pass-through. A capability denial comes back as an MCP tool-level error (`isError: true`) with the typed reason in `details.kind`, not a JSON-RPC error — so the agent surfaces "the substrate refused this" cleanly without treating it as a transport break.

## Philosophy: substrate, not application

FFS doesn't tell you what your knowledge is *for*. It gives you the primitives — atoms, capabilities, federation, projection — and lets applications above the substrate inherit them. The first application planned on top is **Folodex**, a contact-graph tool that exercises FFS for the relationship-holder use case (salespeople, journalists, founders, community organizers who own networks they currently don't control).

But Folodex is one application. The same primitives handle general knowledge capture, AI-agent output absorption, and team collaboration. That breadth is intentional: tools that solve one of these concerns well already exist; what's missing is the substrate underneath that handles all of them coherently.

**FFS aligns with [AARM](https://aarm.dev)** — Autonomous Action Runtime Management — an open specification for securing AI-driven actions at runtime. The mapping is by construction, not retrofit: capability-as-data is AARM's policy engine; atoms are the context accumulator; the proposal-quarantine flow is the approval service; signed-and-multihashed atoms are the receipt generator. See [`ARCHITECTURE.md` § Security model](ARCHITECTURE.md#security-model-aarm-conformant) for the component-by-component breakdown.

## Onboarding

The MVP closes the loop on the technical-friend-onboarding-a-non-technical-peer scenario from the PRD. Three documents under [`docs/onboarding/`](docs/onboarding/) cover the full path from install to daily use:

- [**Technical-friend checklist**](docs/onboarding/technical-friend-checklist.md) — install, keychain, identity, first run, federation handshake. ~45–60 minutes.
- [**First-use guide**](docs/onboarding/first-use-guide.md) — capture, navigate, review, edit, federate. Audience is the end-user peer; no terminal use required.
- [**Troubleshooting**](docs/onboarding/troubleshooting.md) — every known failure mode with symptoms and fixes (SQLCipher, Windows named-pipe, federation handshake, skill subprocess hangs, capability denials).

Annotated illustrations of the Obsidian-side surfaces live in [`docs/onboarding/screenshots/`](docs/onboarding/screenshots/).

## Follow along

This project is being built in the open. There is nothing to install yet; the most useful things you can do today are:

- ⭐ Star the repo — signals interest and helps surface it.
- 👀 Watch for releases — first usable build is what we're heading toward.
- 📖 Read [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) and the [PRD](.compozy/tasks/ffs-mvp/_prd.md). They're the substantive design.
- 💬 Open a [Discussion](https://github.com/Fornado-Greenhouse/ffs/discussions) — especially with use-case signal: *"here's the network I'd want to share — does FFS fit?"*
- 🐛 File an [Issue](https://github.com/Fornado-Greenhouse/ffs/issues) for design feedback, technical concerns, or "I'd like to use this for X."

`CONTRIBUTING.md` and `SECURITY.md` are forthcoming. For security concerns in the meantime, contact the maintainer directly. Operational norms for working in this repo (test runner, shell discipline, ADR numbering) are documented in [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md).

## License and credit

FFS is licensed under the [Blue Oak Model License 1.0.0](LICENSE) — a modern, plain-English permissive license with an explicit patent grant. You may use, copy, modify, and redistribute it freely; please retain the license notice.

Project lead: **Wes Foley**.

Built with the records-not-files lineage of [Datomic](https://www.datomic.com/), [iCloud Notes](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT205773), and the local-first community's push toward user-owned knowledge. The substrate's storage layer rests on [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), and we carry forward its blessing:

> *May you do good and not evil.*
> *May you find forgiveness for yourself and forgive others.*
> *May you share freely, never taking more than you give.*
